1:
Gregory the Great takes the reply as a lesson in how to argue. Men in the heat of opposition attack whatever they hear from an opponent, right or wrong, because a speaker who is unwelcome makes even the truth unwelcome; whereas the good, whose dislike falls on the fault and not on the man, condemn what is amiss while still adopting whatever was rightly said. They sit, he says, as the most even umpires of an opponent's meaning. His figure is agricultural: among a wilderness of thorns an ear of corn will generally be found growing from good seed, and the tiller must work so that the thorn is pulled while the ear is spared.

Gill and Henry both notice what Job does not say. Gill observes that he takes no notice of Bildad's harsh expressions or his unfriendliness, but goes straight into the argument, granting some things and confuting others. Henry points out that Bildad had opened by rebuking Job for talking so much, which would have been easy enough to throw back at him, and that Job lets it go; and he draws the rule from it — we should be ready to own how far we agree with those we dispute against, and should not slight, much less resist, a truth because an adversary produced it and urged it against us, even where it was misapplied.

What Job means by conceding it is genuinely disputed. Henry reports one reading, that the words are a passionate complaint of God's strictness and severity, a protest that here is a God there is no dealing with; and he grants that there are peevish expressions in the chapter. He prefers to take it as a pious confession of man's sinfulness, his own included. Delitzsch reads the concession as irony: Job confirms Bildad's maxim, that what God does is always right — because God does it. Clarke takes it flatly and personally: he acknowledges the general truth of the maxims advanced, and adds that though righteous before men and sincere in his piety, all his righteousness is nothing beside the immaculate holiness of God. Wesley states it without heat: God does ordinarily bless the righteous and punish the wicked, and no man is absolutely just if God marks what is amiss in him.

Delitzsch also fixes whom Job is answering, ruling out a similar earlier speech by Eliphaz and giving the assent to what Bildad has just said. He renders what follows as a challenge rather than a lament: the wise in heart and mighty in strength, who has defied him and remained unhurt.

Who contends with whom in the next verse is left open by one and settled by another. Gill gives both directions: if God contends with man, man cannot answer the allegations produced; or if man contends with God, it is a potsherd striving with its maker, and the match is unequal either way. Ellicott takes man as the subject and offers two senses of the famous phrase — one question out of a thousand, or once in a thousand times. Wesley narrows it to accusation: one charge among the thousand God could produce. Clarke reads it the same way and turns it toward the doctrine he cares most about: of a thousand offences a man cannot vindicate himself in even one, which is why justification by faith and sanctification by the Spirit are so necessary to sinful men.

On the two attributes named next, Gill and Clarke divide the labour. Gill dwells on the wisdom: God is wise originally and essentially, his understanding infinite, able to traverse every scheme and see every thought and action, public or private. Clarke joins the second term to the first and makes the pair a threat rather than a wonder — by his knowledge he searches out all things, and by his power he can punish all delinquencies.
5:
Whether the removing of mountains is meant literally is where the two commentators part. Clarke takes it for earthquakes, in which mountains, valleys, hills and even whole islands are carried off in an instant; and he fastens on the clause they know not as recording the suddenness of it, the work done in the twinkling of an eye with no warning given. Gill keeps several senses open at once. He allows a literal one and produces evidence — a village in Helvetia swallowed up in the fall of a mountain, with eighteen hundred inhabitants and no trace left; a prophecy of the mount of Olives splitting north and south, which Josephus reports as fact; and the deluge, which covered the highest hills and may well have washed some out of place. He also allows the words to be proverbial rather than physical.

On the next line Gill turns the other way and rules Clarke's reading out. The shaking of the earth out of her place cannot mean ordinary earthquakes, he says, which are partial and move only a portion of the surface; it belongs either to the last day, when the earth will reel like a drunkard and be removed like a cottage, or to the flood, after which the earth received some alteration in its situation — a view he takes from Burnet and finds supported by the apostle's distinction between the present earth and the former.

The sun that does not rise is given five explanations, four of them by Gill alone. It may be what God could do if he chose, as when he made the sun stand still in Joshua's day and brought the shadow back on the dial for Hezekiah; or it may mean that the sun rises only when and where he commands; or it may describe eclipses, or a sky so overcast for days together that the sun seems not to have risen; or it may recall the three days' darkness in Egypt, which fell about Job's own period; or, as he rather prefers, the forty days of rain in the deluge, through which the sun never appeared. Clarke compresses all of this into clouds, thick darkness, or an eclipse, and spends his attention instead on the sealing of the stars — sealed, he says, like the contents of a letter wrapped and closed so that it cannot be read, since the heavens sometimes turn as black as ebony and not one star or character in that great book of God can be made out.

The spreading of the heavens Gill takes as a continuing act rather than a past one. The word means expanse, so named from being spread out; it is stretched like a curtain, or like a tent to live in, and Gill suggests a military tent in particular, the pavilion of a general from which the Lord plays his artillery on his enemies with thunder, lightning, hailstones and coals of fire. What the verse asserts, on his reading, is not the first creation but the maintenance — God continues to hold the heavens spread so that they are not yet rolled up like a scroll, and he does it alone, with no help from angels or men.

The last clause draws out Clarke's admiration and a textual note from Delitzsch. Clarke calls it a very majestic image: God does not merely walk upon the water but, when the sea runs mountains high, steps from billow to billow in his essential majesty, which he sets beside the psalm that has the Lord sitting upon the flood. Delitzsch renders it as walking upon the heights of the sea, and reports that Ewald, Hirzel and others construe the verb for spreading in a different sense altogether, taken from a psalm, so that God would be letting the heavens down rather than stretching them out.
9:
The constellations are identified with some care and some hesitation. Gill insists the first name is not a single star but a group, following two Jewish commentators, and points to the older phrase about that constellation and his sons, he notes that another rabbi took it for the seven stars, but rules that out because the Pleiades are named separately just after. His placing is precise: about the northern pole, in the tail of the Bear, appearing in early September and bringing stormy weather. Delitzsch renders the four names and lets them stand: the Bear, Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the south.

What follows is more interesting than a list, and both Ellicott and Wesley notice why. The clause about doing great things past finding out is not Job's own phrasing: it is word for word what Eliphaz had said earlier in the argument. Wesley presses it — the agreement is in the original and in the very same words, and the repetition is deliberate, to show how fully Job agrees with his opponents about the divine perfections. Ellicott finds the same borrowing again a verse later, in the words about God passing on, which Eliphaz had also used. Job conducts his defence in his accusers' vocabulary.

The invisibility is then stated at three depths. Clarke puts it briefly: God is incomprehensible in all his ways, and must be so if he is God and works as God. Gill sets out the degrees — the angels behold his face, men see his eternal power in creation, the saints see his countenance by faith in the word and in Christ, and in heaven will see him as he is — then says what none of that reaches: his essence is invisible, not merely unseen by bodily eyes but incapable of being comprehended in the mind. Delitzsch turns the same thought toward government rather than sight: God works among men as he works in nature, with supreme control, invisibly, irresistibly, and is answerable to no one.

Ellicott adds the observation that gives the passage its edge. Job is depicting, in words of great sublimity, the unapproachable majesty of a God omnipotent and invisible, and showing how hopeless it is to enter into judgment with him; and he notes that although this is a proposition to which everyone assents, scarcely any is so often repudiated in practice, men still casting about to justify themselves before God.

On what God takes away, Gill draws a line the chapter itself does not draw. There are things God never takes from his people — his love, his grace once wrought in them, his gift of Christ, the spiritual blessings, all of them irreversible; but temporal things he removes at pleasure, and in Job's case had removed the children, the servants, the substance and the health. When it pleases him, Gill adds on the authority of the Targum, he takes the man himself out of the world.

The last clause of the section is the one nobody can settle. Delitzsch renders it as the helpers of Rahab stooping beneath him, and takes the verse to mean that God does not restrain his anger until it has accomplished its purpose. Ellicott gives the literal phrase and then admits defeat on it: whether Rahab stands for Egypt or is a poetical name for the fallen archangel is impossible to say, and if the former there is probably an allusion to the overthrow of Pharaoh and his hosts, but the evidence to make that plain is lacking. Gill reads the anger pastorally, distinguishing the anger God seems to bear his own people while he afflicts them, which does not last, from the anger he bears the wicked every day and never withdraws. Clarke states the practical upshot in a line: it is of no use to contend with God, who cannot be successfully resisted.
14:
Henry turns the argument back on the speaker and then asks where the despair comes from. Job has been describing man's general inability to contend with God, and now applies it to himself, in effect giving up hope of gaining God's favour. Henry knows the unkind explanation — that it springs from hard thoughts of God, as of one who, having set himself against Job, would prove too strong — and sets it aside. He prefers to trace it to Job's sense of the imperfection of his own righteousness, and to the dark and cloudy apprehensions of God that he had at that moment.

Gill measures the disproportion in the same terms Job uses. There is no disputing a point with one who is wise in heart and mighty in strength, invisible, able to come at a man from any side unawares, and sovereign to do whatever he pleases; and if the proud tyrants of the earth and the infernal powers are made to stoop, a poor and feeble creature cannot enter the lists. What Gill hears is proportion rather than despair: Job speaking as meanly of himself as he had spoken highly of God.

On the next line Gill draws a distinction the verse does not make and the rest of the book depends on. When Job says that though he were righteous he would not answer, he is not speaking of the righteousness of his cause, which he meant to hold fast as long as he lived; nor of the righteousness of his living Redeemer, by which Gill says he knew he would be justified, and pleading which a man answers every demand of the law. He speaks only of his own legal and civil righteousness, of being good as men reckon goodness. Clarke reaches the same place without the machinery: though clear of every crime, public and secret, that his friends charge him with, he would not dare stand before immaculate holiness, since a man's holiness may profit men but is nothing in the sight of infinite purity. Clarke then quotes a hymn to the effect that the sight of God makes the poet loathe himself and fall into nothing, content that God be exalted.

The verse about calling and being answered is read two ways, and Gill supplies both. Broughton turned it into a question — if I cry, will he answer me? — as though Job doubted whether God would reply at all, the hand having lain on him so long. The other rendering makes it past tense: though I have called, and he has answered. Gill notes that the second fits the man, since Job had prayed in his closet and in his family, and had found God hear; the doubt is whether he would hear now. Wesley takes the doubt further still, so that even an answer would not convince: Job could not believe his desire had really been granted while he remained covered with the tokens of displeasure, and would conclude it had been a pleasant dream rather than a real thing. Clarke reads the same hesitation as evidence in Job's favour, and says so bluntly — sentiments like these sufficiently confute the slander of his friends, who called him presumptuous and said he had no becoming notion of the majesty of God.

The tempest that breaks him is given a local colour by Gill. It rises suddenly and carries everything before it, and Gill wonders whether Job has in mind the storm that brought the house down on his children. He then reports Schultens, who renders the word as a burning tempest of the kind travellers describe in the east, which kills a man outright, blackens his flesh like a coal, and leaves it coming away from the bones in the hand that tries to lift him. On that reading, Gill says, a man is broken to pieces indeed.
18:
Not being suffered to take breath is explained three ways, and only one of them is medical. Gill reports that some refer it to Job's disease, an asthma or quinsy that made breathing hard, but prefers the hot winds of those countries, quoting a traveller who met between Suez and Cairo a wind so hot that the party had to turn their backs to it to take a little breath. What the phrase really does, on Gill's reading, is measure the frequency of the blows: they came so thick that there was no breathing time between them. Clarke says the same without the wind — no respite, the body suffering continually and the mind harassed without pause. Ellicott attends to the action itself: breathing again after complete exhaustion, the recovery of breath and of the power to breathe.

Clarke then makes an observation that reorganises the whole stretch of the speech. Almost all the terms Job uses from here on are forensic, taken from legal process and from pleadings in the gate, the court of justice of that world. On that footing he re-renders a clause: where the English asks who shall set me a time, Clarke asks who would be a witness for me, or dare appear on my behalf. The complaint is not that God is unreachable but that the case is unarguable for want of anyone to conduct it.

The two heads of that case are strength and judgment, and Gill takes the first at its word. A man might hope to carry a point by force, as men do by the authority they possess; but Job is a weak creature in body, mind and estate, and God is the most strong, so there is nothing to be done on that side. Ellicott calls the passage the most uncompromising acknowledgment of man's inability to stand in judgment before God, while admitting its expression is abrupt to the point of being enigmatic.

On the second head the witnesses converge on a paradox. Ellicott states it as a rule: to say I am perfect is itself the act that proves a man perverse. Clarke comes at it from the other side — God must have some reason for his conduct, so Job will not pretend to justify himself, the attempt being an insult to God's majesty and justice; and yet Clarke will not concede the charge, since Job is conscious of none of the crimes alleged and does not know why God contends with him, only that a reason exists which God does not explain. Wesley reduces the clause to its bare sense, pleading one's own righteousness and innocency against God. Gill notes that the perfection supposed is only supposed — a man conscious of no sin in thought, word or deed — so that Job argues from a case, not a claim.

Delitzsch then reports a genuine division over what Job actually says next. The usual view, which he names four scholars for holding, makes the line an affirmation of innocence flung out at the risk of everything: I am innocent, and I say it boldly even in scorn of my life. Delitzsch prefers the plainer sense of the Hebrew, which is that Job does not know his own soul — does not know himself. On that reading the contradiction between his innocence and his lot has made his own self-consciousness look deceptive; he has become a stranger to himself, and it is this life of seeming contradictions that he cannot bear and does not wish prolonged. The difference carries into the next line as well. Delitzsch will not render it as meaning that it is all the same to Job whether he lives or dies, but as meaning that it is all one whether a man is innocent or not — of which, as he says, Job takes himself to be the proof.
22:
The opening words are rendered four ways and Gill collects them all. One takes them as there is one thing in the world; the Targum makes it one measure dealt to good and bad alike; a third gives it is all one, so that a man righteous or not is equally liable to affliction; and Broughton has this is uniform, which Gill reads either of God acting uniformly or of Job being steady in a view he had not departed from. Gill adds the point that matters: this was where Job differed from his three friends, and not on the justice of God, which he granted them and believed even here, though he could not account for it. Delitzsch renders the line as a conclusion rather than an observation — there is one thing, therefore I maintain it — and takes the one thing to be that it is all one whether a man is innocent or not.

What the scourge is gets a careful answer. Gill rules out the reading that makes it Satan, found in two Jewish commentators, and takes it for any calamity that lashes like a whip — sword, famine, pestilence, wild beasts — coming suddenly and unlooked for. He notes that these are sometimes a father's chastisement and more often sent in displeasure, that one Greek version restricts the clause to the wicked, and that on one reading those killed outright fare better than those left to linger.

Ellicott does not soften what the verse then says. The sense, he thinks, is that when hidden calamity overtakes an innocent man God will laugh at it — will take no more notice of it than if it furnished him with sport; and the mere fact that such calamity befalls the innocent, when providence could easily interpose, looks like indifference, as though he winked at it. But Ellicott places the argument rather than endorsing it: this is the reasoning of a man deliberately shutting faith out of his estimate of God's dealings — not that Job lacks faith, but that his friends have staked everything on the strict justice of God, and he confronts them with the severe logic of facts which they can neither contradict nor explain. For the purposes of the argument he takes the darkest view available.

Who holds the earth is answered three ways by Gill without a decision. It may be Satan, as the same two commentators held; or some tyrant, a Nimrod or another known to Job; or simply wicked men in general, who hold most of the earth and most of the power in it. What Gill will not allow is any inference from it. Whatever such men have, they have from God, the powers that be being ordained by him; but it is only the things of this world, and that is their whole portion — so the giving of these is no proof that a man is good and the taking of them away no evidence that he is wicked. Love and hatred, Gill says, are not to be known by these things.

Clarke states the same as a plain fact of experience: the worst men possess most of this world's goods and the righteous are scarcely ever in power; it was so in Job's time and is so still, so prosperity and adversity are marks of neither approval nor disapproval. On the harder clause that follows he offers two ways out. The first is a rule of scriptural idiom — God is often said to do what he only permits, so that he permits the eyes of judgment to be blinded and false decisions follow. The second is a rendering he takes from Good, in which the agent is not God at all: the earth is given over to the hand of Injustice, and it is she who hoodwinks the faces of its judges.
25:
Henry marks a change of temperature here and does not excuse it. Job grows more and more querulous, and does not end the chapter with the reverent language about God's wisdom and justice that he began with; and Henry generalises the warning — those who indulge a complaining humour do not know what indecencies it will hurry them into, the beginning of such strife being like the letting out of water, so that it should be left off before it is meddled with. The distinction he insists on is between complaining to God, which the Psalmist does often and which is allowed, and complaining of God, which Henry says is what Job does here. He is careful, though, to exempt the opening of the passage: the lament over the passing of prosperous days is proper enough.

How fast those days went is described by a figure that the commentators render in several ways. Gill takes the first comparison as a runner in a race, or a courier carrying a message on foot or on horseback, and says Job's days outran them; and following Broughton he limits the days to the prosperous ones, which came and were gone. Henry uses the same image and names the two runners from the old history who carried news to David, saying no express ever made such haste as Job's comforts did in leaving him, and that no trace of his prosperity remains any more than of an eagle in the air or a ship in the sea.

The ships themselves are disputed. Gill gives three possibilities: the lightest-built vessels; or, following a Jewish commentator, ships rowed with oars, which may be called ships of will or of desire because they can be taken anywhere at pleasure while sailing vessels must wait on the wind; or else ships of enmity, pirate craft, fast because they carry no cargo. Delitzsch supplies a fourth by rendering the phrase as ships of reeds, and puts the eagle beside it as one that dashes upon its prey.

The resolution to cheer up is examined word by word. Clarke glosses the first clause as forgoing the complaint altogether, and reports the Latin version of the second, which turns it into changing the countenance — forcing a smile and assuming the appearance of comfort. Delitzsch renders it in the same direction, giving up the dark looks and putting on a cheerful face. Gill fills in what would have to be forgotten: the children, the servants, the substance and the health, buried in oblivion so that the note might be changed.

Why the resolution fails is stated by all three of the remaining witnesses in their own idiom. Gill has him afraid that the sorrows will return, surround him and overwhelm him, so that he will never be released. Wesley finds the endeavour vain for a subtler reason — grief may be suspended for a time, but the fear does not stop; and he reads the closing clause as Job's perception that God will not clear his innocence by removing the afflictions that make his friends judge him guilty of some great crime. Wesley's verdict on the sentence is as blunt as Henry's: words proceeding from despair and impatience.

Clarke closes with two places where he parts from the older versions. Coverdale, following the Latin, has Job afraid of all his works rather than all his sorrows, which Clarke reports with some sympathy — even if he ceased complaining he might fear that not one of his works, however well intended, would stand God's scrutiny. On the last clause, though, he refuses the version outright: to render it as a statement that God does not favour an evildoer is not the sense of the original, which means that God will not acquit Job so as to take his afflictions away from him.
29:
The labour that would be in vain is understood two ways. Gill gives the first on a Jewish commentator's authority: if Job really were the hypocrite his friends take him for, then praying would be wasted effort, since God does not hear men who keep iniquity in the heart — and Gill notes in passing that prayer is fitly called labour, being a striving and wrestling with God when it is constant and fervent. He prefers a second sense, that the vanity lies not in Job's guilt but in God's reckoning: if he is counted a wicked man, or simply dealt with as one, then nothing he does will alter the case. Clarke takes it in the first direction and applies it to the resolution just abandoned — if he is the sinner they suppose, it is useless to counterfeit joy and leave off complaining.

The snow water is given a physical explanation before a moral one. Gill notes that it came either straight from the sky or off the snow-covered mountains, or was kept in vessels for the purpose, and that the ancients used it as a wash because it whitens the skin and tightens the pores. What the figure says, on his reading, is that no method of self-cleansing will serve: neither the ceremonial washings that may have been in use in Job's time, which sanctify only to the purifying of the flesh, nor moral duties, nor even repentance, which Gill mentions on another commentator's authority. Delitzsch renders the pair of clauses with a second cleanser beside the first, washing with snow water and making the hands clean with lye.

What Job would be plunged into afterwards is also read two ways, and Gill gives both without choosing. It may be the ditch of sin — the horrible pit, the mire and clay, in which a self-righteous man is shown at last to have been standing all along, notwithstanding the purity he boasts of; Job being none of those things, the point would be that set beside the perfect holiness of God he must appear exceedingly impure. Or the ditch may be the ditch of afflictions, which is how Gill reports another expositor taking it: either the present ulcers and scabs covering his body, or fresh troubles still to be sent. Delitzsch's rendering suits the second, with the plunging into the pit followed by the clothes themselves abhorring the man who wears them.
32:
Why no answer is possible is stated first as a difference of kind. Gill explains that the hands and eyes scripture gives to God are said after the manner of men, there being something in him that figuratively answers to them; in himself he is a spirit, infinite, immortal, invisible, pure and without iniquity, while Job is finite, feeble, mortal and sinful. Potsherds, Gill says, may contend with the potsherds of the earth, their equals, but not with their Creator, who sees impurity where a man sees none and can bring and sustain a charge where the man thought there was nothing to charge. Wesley puts the same in half a line: not a man, but one infinitely superior in majesty and power.

The famous word in the next verse is worth the space both Gill and Clarke give it. Gill offers two senses — one that reproves, rebuking the party in the wrong, or an umpire to whom the case may be referred — and then quotes the observation that settles why there is none: a man standing between two parties must be both wiser and mightier than either, and nobody is wiser or mightier than God. Clarke works on the English rather than the Hebrew. A daysman in English law is an arbitrator or umpire, so called from the bestowing of a day on which a matter is decided, day being the legal term for the appointed time of appearance in court; but arbitrator, he says, is the proper meaning here — one appointed by the consent of both sides. Delitzsch's rendering keeps the physical gesture that the English loses, an arbitrator who should lay his hand upon them both.

The rod Job wants lifted divides the two commentators, and the disagreement is not small. Gill is emphatic that it is not the rod as an ensign of government, since Job had no wish to be freed from God's rule, but the rod of affliction, the stroke of the hand that lay so heavily on him that he could not reason freely while it remained. Clarke allows the other sense: the word means sceptre as well as rod, so Job may be picturing God seated in majesty on the judgment seat, a sight so appalling that it left him unable to speak — and Clarke draws the general rule out of it, that when a sinful soul sees God in his majesty, terror seizes it and prayer becomes impossible.

Clarke also preserves a scribal curiosity no other witness mentions. In the Masoretic Bibles the word for his rod is written with an oversized letter; and since that letter stands for nine when letters are used as numerals, the Masora explains the enlargement as marking the nine calamities under which Job had suffered and which he was asking God to remove.

What Job would do if the rod were lifted is read at two levels. Gill allows a devotional sense first — that with the rod of the law and the terror of justice removed, and grace shown through the Mediator, a believer may speak boldly at the throne of grace without servile fear, though still with reverence. But he thinks Job's own meaning is the plainer and less comfortable one: with the dread of that majesty taken off, he could state his case properly and defend himself, which he cannot do while it presses on him. Gill adds the sequel from later in the book: these were bold and daring expressions, and Job blushed for them once he was made sensible of it. Clarke ends on the clause that closes the chapter, taking it to mean simply that Job is not in circumstances that allow him to plead with his Judge, and Delitzsch's rendering leaves it there: then would I speak and not fear him, but it is not so with me.
